classification.difficultyReason: Apply the null factor law to supplied factors and solve the resulting linear equations, including fractional roots.

questions.mappingNote: All twelve parts already supply a product equal to zero. Apply the null factor law directly and solve each variable factor; nonzero numerical factors introduce no additional solutions.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 introduces the null factor law and applies it to factored quadratic equations. Page 3 warns against dividing by a variable and losing the zero root. Page 4 Example 4 includes linear factors with non-unit coefficients; page 5 distinguishes nonzero numerical common factors.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the null factor law to supplied factors and solve the resulting linear equations, including fractional roots.

classification.difficultyReason: Extract a common variable factor and apply the null factor law, first rearranging two equations and retaining the zero solution.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–d directly require a common variable factor. Parts e–f first require rearrangement to zero. Every part assesses solving a quadratic with a common variable factor, rather than general trinomial factorisation.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 states the null factor law and Example 1a extracts a common variable factor. Page 3 Example 3a first moves all terms to the left, then factorises; its note warns that cancelling the variable loses the zero solution.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Extract a common variable factor and apply the null factor law, first rearranging two equations and retaining the zero solution.

classification.difficultyReason: Factor monic trinomials with integer factors, including repeated factors, and apply the null factor law.

questions.mappingNote: All fifteen parts are monic quadratic equations already equal to zero. Each uses Example 1b directly; d, l and o have equal factors and one distinct solution. The supplied reuse candidate has a different complete question and is ineligible for reuse.
questions.methodNote: Example 1b finds two numbers with the required product and sum, factorises the monic trinomial, sets each factor equal to zero and solves. The summary on page 4 states the null factor law. Examples 3–5 reinforce rearranging and factorising.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Factor monic trinomials with integer factors, including repeated factors, and apply the null factor law.

classification.difficultyReason: Rearrange equations before factorising, retain zero roots and recognise when a square cannot equal a negative number.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and g use common-variable factors; b, c, e, h, j and k use monic factorisation after rearrangement; d, f and i require the non-negative-square argument; l follows Example 2a directly.
questions.methodNote: Examples 1 and 3 rearrange to zero, factorise and apply the null factor law without dividing by the variable. Example 2 solves a positive square equation directly and explains why a negative square has no real solution. Pages 4–5 reinforce these methods.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Rearrange equations before factorising, retain zero roots and recognise when a square cannot equal a negative number.

classification.difficultyReason: Divide by the numerical common factor, factorise the resulting monic trinomial and apply the null factor law.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a, b and c require division by 2, 3 and 4 respectively. Each then directly assesses solving a monic quadratic by factorisation. The supplied reuse candidate has different equations and a different complete part set, so whole-question reuse is unsuitable.
questions.methodNote: Example 5a first divides both sides by a numerical common factor, then factorises the monic trinomial and sets each factor equal to zero. Example 1b explains selecting factors using their product and sum.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Divide by the numerical common factor, factorise the resulting monic trinomial and apply the null factor law.

classification.difficultyReason: Factorise non-monic quadratics, rearranging some equations before applying the null factor law.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–h, n, o and q directly assess non-monic factorisation; i–m, p and r additionally require rearrangement. Every part fits solve-quadratic-factorisation. The offered reuse candidate has different equations and a different complete part set, so it is ineligible.
questions.methodNote: Move all terms to the left, split the middle term using two numbers whose product is ac and sum is b, factorise in pairs, then apply the null factor law. Example 4 explicitly demonstrates non-monic factorisation; Example 5 reinforces rearrangement.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Factorise non-monic quadratics, rearranging some equations before applying the null factor law.

classification.difficultyReason: Simplify by a numerical common factor, factorise non-monic quadratics by splitting the middle term, and apply the null factor law.

questions.mappingNote: All twelve parts require non-monic quadratic factorisation after numerical simplification; f also requires rearrangement. The offered reuse candidate has different equations and parts and is not source-equivalent.
questions.methodNote: Divide both sides by the numerical common factor first. Rearrange to zero where necessary, split the middle term, factorise in pairs and apply the null factor law, following Example 5b and Example 4.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Simplify by a numerical common factor, factorise non-monic quadratics by splitting the middle term, and apply the null factor law.

classification.difficultyReason: Select and link familiar expansion, rearrangement and factorisation procedures, including non-monic factors; retain the zero root in g and recognise the negative square in e as having no real solution.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a, b and h require monic factorisation; c and j require non-monic factorisation; d and i isolate squares; e produces a negative square; f requires expanding both sides; g retains the zero solution through common-factor factorisation; k uses a common binomial factor; l first clears the numerical denominator. General quadratic factorisation is the most advanced directly assessed supplied skill.
questions.methodNote: Examples 6 and 7 demonstrate forming a quadratic in standard form, factorising and applying the null factor law. Example 8 demonstrates expansion and collecting terms after clearing denominators. Apply the same equivalent-equation method here; use square roots for isolated squares.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select and link familiar expansion, rearrangement and factorisation procedures, including non-monic factors; retain the zero root in g and recognise the negative square in e as having no real solution.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose a common denominator, expand and collect terms, then factorise and check excluded values; the hardest parts link these taught procedures without requiring a new representation.

questions.mappingNote: Every part requires clearing a pronumeral denominator. Parts a–i and k–n additionally use quadratic factorisation; j simplifies to a linear equation after clearing its common denominator. These are algebraic-denominator equations rather than compound-fraction simplification tasks.
questions.methodNote: Example 6 clears powers of x from denominators, rearranges and factorises, then checks solutions in the original equation. Example 7 uses cross-multiplication. Example 8 multiplies by the product of binomial denominators and expands before collecting terms. Exclude denominator-zero values throughout.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Choose a common denominator, expand and collect terms, then factorise and check excluded values; the hardest parts link these taught procedures without requiring a new representation.

classification.difficultyReason: Part a scaffolds the length as 50/x; use the diagram and equal square sides to equate this to x+5, then form and factorise the quadratic and reject the negative width.

questions.mappingNote: Part a uses area to express a side algebraically. Part b models the square condition, clears the denominator and solves a monic quadratic by factorisation; contextual modelling is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Examples 6–8 clear algebraic denominators by multiplying both sides, rearrange, and factorise where a quadratic remains. Use the null factor law and check admissibility in the original context.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Part a scaffolds the length as 50/x; use the diagram and equal square sides to equate this to x+5, then form and factorise the quadratic and reject the negative width.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute into a supplied formula, solve the resulting quadratic by factorisation and reject the negative number of sides.

questions.mappingNote: This question uses the same polygon formula and modelling sequence as Example 9, with 44 diagonals instead of 35. The most advanced directly assessed skill is quadratic modelling.
questions.methodNote: The introduction on page 9 explains that algebraic solutions must be checked against the real-world context. Example 9 on page 10 substitutes the number of diagonals into D=n(n-3)/2, multiplies by 2, rearranges to a monic quadratic, factorises, applies the null factor law and rejects the negative number of sides.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute into a supplied formula, solve the resulting quadratic by factorisation and reject the negative number of sides.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate related rectangle dimensions and a given area into a quadratic, factorise and select the positive dimension.

questions.mappingNote: Question 2 assesses the same rectangle-area model as Example 10, with a difference of 4 cm and area 96 cm², and asks for the longer side.
questions.methodNote: The introduction on page 9 requires contextual rejection of unsuitable quadratic solutions. Example 10 on page 10 defines the shorter rectangle side, expresses the other side in terms of it, uses area to form a monic quadratic, factorises and rejects the negative length.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate related rectangle dimensions and a given area into a quadratic, factorise and select the positive dimension.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute a specified sum into a supplied formula, solve the resulting quadratic by factorisation and reject the negative root.

questions.methodNote: The introduction on page 9 requires interpreting quadratic solutions in context. Example 9 on page 10 substitutes a given count into a formula, clears the denominator, rearranges, factorises, applies the null factor law and rejects a negative count.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute a specified sum into a supplied formula, solve the resulting quadratic by factorisation and reject the negative root.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate a verbal relationship into a non-monic quadratic, factorise and retain both valid numerical solutions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate a verbal relationship into a non-monic quadratic, factorise and retain both valid numerical solutions.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise perfect-square trinomials and solve their repeated linear factors, including fractional and non-monic cases.

questions.mappingNote: Every part is a perfect-square quadratic. Parts a–h have monic factors, including fractional constants; parts i–n require non-monic binomial factors, as in Example 11b. Example 14 is not needed for this task.
questions.methodNote: Example 11 factors each perfect-square trinomial into a repeated binomial, writes its square equal to zero and solves the linear factor. Its note permits factorisation on inspection using the perfect-square identities.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise perfect-square trinomials and solve their repeated linear factors, including fractional and non-monic cases.

classification.difficultyReason: Match expressions to the two taught special-product patterns, checking the middle term for perfect squares, recognising reordered terms and rejecting near matches.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed task is recognition of special-product expansions, rather than solving equations or completing the square. The closest catalogue skill is factorise-special-products.
questions.methodNote: Page 12 explicitly gives both perfect-square identities and recognises perfect squares by inspection. Page 3 demonstrates factorisation using the difference-of-two-squares identity. Pages 13–14 provide the surrounding completing-the-square context.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Match expressions to the two taught special-product patterns, checking the middle term for perfect squares, recognising reordered terms and rejecting near matches.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the square of half the linear coefficient to monic expressions, including odd and negative coefficients.

questions.mappingNote: Every assigned part asks only for the missing constant in a monic perfect square. Parts a–e use even coefficients; f–i use odd coefficients and exact fractions. The closest directly assessed skill is complete-square-form.
questions.methodNote: Example 12 on PDF page 13 takes half the coefficient of x and squares it, then verifies the resulting perfect-square identity. Page 12 introduces the same rule.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the square of half the linear coefficient to monic expressions, including odd and negative coefficients.

classification.difficultyReason: Complete monic squares with positive, negative and odd linear coefficients, retaining exact fractions.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly applies Example 13 to a monic expression. Page 12 introduces the same method; page 14 confirms Exercise 5D. The non-monic Example 14c inconsistency is irrelevant to these monic tasks and was not used.
questions.methodNote: Example 13 adds and subtracts the square of half the linear coefficient, then rewrites the perfect-square trinomial and simplifies the constant. Exact fractions are retained for odd coefficients.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Complete monic squares with positive, negative and odd linear coefficients, retaining exact fractions.

classification.difficultyReason: Complete the square for non-monic expressions, including negative leading coefficients and fractional shifts.

questions.mappingNote: Every part assesses rewriting a non-monic quadratic in completed-square form, rather than solving an equation. Example 14a–b and the valid algebraic procedure provide the method; the inconsistent sign in Example 14c is not propagated.
questions.methodNote: Example 14 factors out the coefficient of x squared, adds and subtracts the square of half the resulting linear coefficient, forms the binomial square, then distributes the outside coefficient. Examples 12–13 establish the half-coefficient method.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Complete the square for non-monic expressions, including negative leading coefficients and fractional shifts.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Complete the square with even integer linear coefficients and simplify exact surds.

questions.methodNote: Example 16b: add the square of half the odd linear coefficient, retain fractions, then take both square roots.

questions.methodNote: Example 17: move the constant, divide by the leading coefficient, add the square of half the new linear coefficient and take both roots.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose among the named methods, factorise or complete the square, and interpret a negative square as giving no real solution.

questions.mappingNote: The mixed set explicitly names factorisation and completing the square, and precedes the quadratic-formula introduction. Completing the square is the most advanced directly assessed method.
questions.methodNote: Use the null factor law after factorisation where convenient; otherwise complete the square. A negative completed square proves there is no real solution.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Choose among the named methods, factorise or complete the square, and interpret a negative square as giving no real solution.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand products or clear denominators, then complete the square or factorise; check that rational-equation roots are nonzero. These are routine linked procedures using the taught methods.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–e require completing the square after rearrangement; c–f also assess clearing pronumeral denominators, and f factorises after clearing 3x.
questions.methodNote: Expand products or multiply by denominators with x≠0, then complete the square or factorise. The rearrangements are reversible on the stated domain.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand products or clear denominators, then complete the square or factorise; check that rational-equation roots are nonzero. These are routine linked procedures using the taught methods.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute signed coefficients into the quadratic formula and simplify exact roots, including extracting square factors.

questions.mappingNote: All nine parts directly assess the quadratic formula with exact answers. Parts a, g, h and i require extracting square factors; b and d give integer roots; c, e and f retain irreducible surds. No supplied reuse candidate has the same complete task.
questions.methodNote: Example 18 identifies a, b and c, calculates b²−4ac, substitutes into both branches of the quadratic formula, simplifies surds and cancels common factors. The authored ± notation retains both branches. Example 18b's repeated plus branch is a source typo; its preceding general minus branch supplies the valid method.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute signed coefficients into the quadratic formula and simplify exact roots, including extracting square factors.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute non-monic coefficients into the quadratic formula and simplify exact roots, including common factors and surds.

questions.mappingNote: All nine parts explicitly require the quadratic formula for non-monic quadratics. Parts a, c, g, h and i additionally simplify surds and common factors; d and e yield rational roots. The offered reuse candidates have different stems, givens and assessed tasks.
questions.methodNote: Identify a, b and c, calculate b²−4ac, substitute into the quadratic formula, simplify the square root and cancel common factors, as in Example 18. The erroneous repeated plus branch in Example 18b is not used; the preceding formula and Example 18c supply valid signs.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute non-monic coefficients into the quadratic formula and simplify exact roots, including common factors and surds.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute signed coefficients into the quadratic formula, evaluate both branches and round irrational roots to two decimal places.

questions.mappingNote: All nine parts directly assess the quadratic formula. Parts c and e give integer roots; the other seven require decimal approximation. The unrelated reuse suggestions do not reproduce this source task. Example 18b's erroneous repeated plus branch is not used.
questions.methodNote: Identify a, b and c, calculate the discriminant, substitute into both branches of the quadratic formula, and retain exact arithmetic until the final decimal approximation. Example 19 on page 21 demonstrates rounding both roots to two decimal places. Exact integer roots remain exact.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute signed coefficients into the quadratic formula, evaluate both branches and round irrational roots to two decimal places.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret the sign of the discriminant and distinguish rational from irrational roots using whether a positive discriminant is a perfect square.

questions.mappingNote: Part a interprets the three discriminant signs. Part b applies Example 21's calculation and classification method to each equation, without finding the roots. The discriminant skill directly covers every response.
questions.methodNote: Page 23 defines the discriminant and Example 21 evaluates it before interpreting its sign and perfect-square status. A negative value gives no real solutions, zero gives one rational solution for these rational coefficients, and a positive value gives two rational or irrational solutions according to its square status.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interpret the sign of the discriminant and distinguish rational from irrational roots using whether a positive discriminant is a perfect square.

classification.difficultyReason: Form quadratic equations from reciprocal, area and similar-triangle relationships, then select contextually valid roots.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use segment addition and the supplied product relation to form a quadratic, apply the formula and reject the negative length.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct and compare compound-interest and simple-interest expressions, simplify to a quadratic, and select the positive interest rate.

questions.mappingNote: Quadratic modelling is the most advanced directly assessed skill. The inspected evidence does not teach the prerequisite simple-interest or annually compounded-interest formulas; original teaching evidence for those formulas is still required.

The source evidence inspected does not teach the prerequisite time = distance ÷ speed relationship; this requires independent content-review evidence.
questions.methodNote: Pages 4–5 teach rearranging quadratic equations to zero. Pages 21–22 demonstrate evaluating the discriminant, applying the quadratic formula, simplifying surds and rounding decimal answers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Model two journey times with algebraic denominators, form a quadratic and select the physically valid root.

classification.difficultyReason: Use perimeter to express one side in terms of the other, form an area equation and interpret its two roots as the side lengths.
